Grain crisis

By: Liz Fish | Production

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
South Africa is laying the groundwork in case it needs to import as much as 6.2-million tons of maize after successive seasons of drought threaten the crop in Africa's top producer of the grain, which is usually a net exporter. State-run ports and rail company Transet CEO Siyabonga Gama said "the rail side is not the issue. We have the capacity there to absorb that much maize," he said. He said South Africa's ports were designed mostly to export grain rather than import it, but this hurdle could be overcome. The issue is the import silo capacity so there are a few things that we will need to tweak. It could still be done." But he said this when the estimated import was 4000 million tons. There was hope that some planting could be done early in 2016 but 50% of the 2.55 Million hectares wasn't planted and we already had a poor harvest last year so we have very low stocks



Further information:
The outlook is not good as an El Nino weather system is exacerbating a scorching start to the growing season, following drought conditions in the previous one which shrivelled the crop by a third to 9.94-million tons, the lowest since 2007. This is helping to fuel inflation in Africa's most advanced economy as the white variety of maize is a staple that provides much of South Africa's caloric intake. South Africa's central bank has repeatedly voiced its concern this year about the impact of drought and food prices on the inflation outlook. The March maize contract climbed over 2% to an all-time high of R3 662/t on Tuesday after forecast rain over the weekend in the western part of the maize belt failed to meet expectations. The December contract is fetching R3 705/t, up 75% so far in 2015 and in January 2016 it is R5000/t It it is going to be a very big import year. But aside from the main grain facilities at the ports of Durban and East London, South Africa Gama said Port Elizabeth and Cape Town and even Richards Bay, which is mostly used for coal exports could be used.
The concern is that the railway lines are not in a good state, and we do not have have insufficient storage capacity. What will these additional import cost do to the already financially over burdened farmers? Zimbabwe has also suffered a massive crop failure and will need to import maize which is likely to have to come through South Africa.
There are fears that we could be facing food riots by the end of the year.

Press Release:


Food Insecurity
South Africa could be forced to import as much as 6.2-million tons of maize following successive seasons of drought. A scorching start to the 2016 growing season has dashed any further hope of planting in the new year, exacerbating the need to look abroad for maize. But SA’s ports were primarily designed to export maize and don’t have the capacity to accommodate such large imported quantities, increasing fears that the country could face massive white maize shortages by the end of the year. Carte Blanche investigates.


Script:


Script: At last the rain has come, but it’s too little too late, and still not enough to plant. We knew we were in for an extreme El Nino, but nobody expected it to hit this hard, says Jannie De Villiers CEO of Grain SA
Jannie: “We are on a knife edge. If the rain stops right now we are not going to produce 5 or 6 million tonness then are going to produce 4 or 3 million tonnes. Then we will have to import 8 million tonnes we can’t do that it’s too much for us.
Script: As the representative of over 5 and half thousand farmers he started sounding the alarm in December last year, meeting with Minister of Agriculture Forestry and Fisheries Senzeni Zokwana
Minister: We are highly concerned that why we have been meeting the stakeholders including those who are producing the commodities
Script: Worst off are emerging farmers
Reikie “I was supposed to be planting maize now under irrigation but now because of the rain I can’t do nothing,
Script: Molemi Modise hopes his animals will survive
“We give them winter leeks until the rainy season comes but in this case we have to feed them winter leeks until as long as it goes. It does matter even if the cattle feed from this, this it is useless”
Script: The whole world has been gripped by extreme weather events impacting on crops globally, says agricultural economist and advisor, Dr John Purchase CEO of Agbiz
John Purchase “ We knew the risk of drought is high and we in fact from Agbiz side we engaged the Government in August last year already and told them we foresee problems. So we are in a catastrophic situation.
Script: Earlier in January when the last hope of planting dried up, the import estimates went up from 4 million tonnes to 6 million – it was time to panic
Minister “Had we known what we know now. I am sure I would agree with you..we could have acted earlier This El Nino La Nina situation is going to be with us so we need to plan in advance or use this as a yardstick to say if it comes again two years or one year later we will not be in the same situation that we are in today
Script: The country is facing the very real possibility of food shortages for the first time in 30 years
Chris Schutte “This is the first time in many years, or in our lifetimes, where you come off a small crop and now have a disaster or a crop failure, so it’s not just a typical just a bad rain season, it is close to a disaster for the first time a government in this country, over the past 25, 30 years, will have to manage food security
Script: Chris Schutte CEO of Astral Foods our largest poultry and feed producer says there enough maize in the world for us to import, but it’s going to cost us.
Chris It is not a global disaster, what is a disaster is the South African situation, we don’t have enough stock here so we are going to have to import, which we can do, if we do import, you are now going to import at almost 50 percent more expensive that what you could have imported a year ago
Link: We have had the lowest rainfall in nearly 100 years. A year ago the price of maize was just over R2000 a ton its now approaching 5000 and we are told we may have to import as much as 6 million tonnes and if you do the maths that is upward of 20 billion rand that’s how much trouble we are in
John Purchase: For the importation will believe the private sector will be able to do that and we have also spoken to the reserve bank The Reserves are there to back up this normal trading process but it is going to impact agribusinesses it’s going to impact on the consumer and it is a significant impact on SA
Script: And farmers are currently sitting with the highest debt levels ever, owing the banks over 125 billion rand.
Jannie: How are the farmers going to plant next year because if they’re in debt the land prices will probably drop their security will not be there they might not be able to get a loan and with the exchange rate worsening I think all our inputs have gone up 30 % all of a sudden
Link: South Africa is primarily geared up for the export of grain and not to import it and the real challenge is that even if you can get it through the port as quickly as it arrives, is our road and railway infra-structure up to the task of moving it inland where it needs to go?
Script: Transnet General Manager for Agriculture, Ulrico Davids, says after several meetings with stakeholders, he feels confident that Transnet has the capacity to deliver
Ulrico Davids: Ports in this case will be ustilized as a through put port and not as a storage so that the product can move out of the ports as quickly as possible into a silo space and from there it can be distributed. The planning aspect is going to become critical.
Script: But can they deliver on their promises?
John Purchase “They have given reassurance but we remain concerned , given the history, that it is going to be a real battle to get the grains in over a sustained period over 12 to 18 months.
Script: Currently we can import white maize from the USA, and Mexico, yellow maize, which we generally use for animal feed, from Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay. But El Nino is wreaking havoc with crops in the USA and they supply 70% of the world’s grain, so there is no certainty on the final figures.
Durban, East London, Port Elizabeth, and Cape Town all have grain handling facilities. Maputo and Beira are available to transport maize to Zimbabwe and the region. 2000 Rail trucks have been re-commissioned so the bulk of the grain can move by rail.
Ulrico Davids “we are looking at changing our handling methods. We also have to bring back some additional rail cars but I think most important is our engagement with private sector and terminal operators so that we have one view of what the ports can handle
Script: Durban’s will receive the bulk of the maize. So theoretically we have sufficient capacity but there are many variables to contend with. For example, this 38 000 tonne carrier takes 4 days to unload and if bad weather hits, it brings everything to a standstill. And there isn’t sufficient storage in the harbours, so it will require a slick trucking system to get it moving, and currently there just aren’t enough trucks.
Jannie. “Durban is our most important port, the consumption area is Gauteng and in between we have had received rain so all the those silos might be full of grain. So you need to look at storage elsewhere because our processing facilities don’t have a lot of storage capacity so we need to look at alternative ways so they can keep on offloading.
Script: We normally export maize and imported about half our wheat, so trucks ran at full capacity in both directions
Jannie “Now all the trucks are going to come one way because it is maize and wheat back to Gauteng. Basically your capacity is going to run half empty down and full back
Script: Jannie says the maximum we can import is 6 million tonnes and that is already going to be a massive achievement. Next month, when the final assessment of grain stocks is made, it could be even higher.
Jannie: If there is a strike in the port for a month we might run out of food in some places in the country. Even a small one little thing can stop us from us getting all the food into the country and that can cause a shortage in terms of availability. If availability is the problem that is when you have a disaster, a major disaster
Bongani: Is Government providing adequate leadership on this
Jannie “Not yet, I think the Government are still in a sort of a phase where they gather information because we haven’t seen any action coming forth, they haven’t declared this as disaster yet, I think once that happens then we can measure them against what they can provide.
Link: When food prices sky rocket it is the poorest consumers who are going to be hardest hit already the price of basic foodstuffs like maize and samp has raised by 40% higher with more increases set to come. The situation is going to get a lot tougher before it’s going to get better.
Chris: Poultry prices, which is the cheapest source of meat protein in the country, will most probably have to rise by between 30 and 35 percent just to break even
Bongani: Are we looking at serious situations where we might have food riots, protests and unrest?
Chris: Well the old saying of ‘when the masses are hungry, the rich won’t sleep’ will be tested this year
Script: Farmers fear rural economies are facing a very real threat of collapse, as local communities depend entirely on them.
Jannie: I am not sure how good is our social networks provided by government in keeping all those people going in the rural economy if agriculture is not providing. It’s going to be a huge a struggle
John Purchase “I believe we will be able to negotiate with government a situation to keep productive farmers on the land to ensure that they can produce next year, so that we can recover to a normal situation. This is an extraordinary situation.
Minister: We have spoken to Landbank and IDC to make sure soft loans available or any other from that may be necessary to make sure that they are above. And I hope that the Minister of finance when he announces the budget that there will be a portion that deals with drought alleviation.
Script: The larger producers say they may survive, but emerging farmers are unlikely to because they farm on communal, or state owned land and so can’t access loans. They are not likely to recover from a drought like this.
Jannie “We would have hoped that there would be some contingency in the Governments budget there must be something that you can help farmers especially the cattle guys, the animals are dying one would have expected a quicker reaction”
Minister “With emerging farmers we have already decided to put aside 20% of what we have budgeted for and a figure of R306 million to make sure that we buy feed for the animals we drill boreholes we supply water it is not enough given the scale this has been
Bongani “The Minister has spoken about sums of money that has been prioritised to assist farmers is that going to be enough?
Jannie “if you look at the ‘92 drought there was about 3.5 billion rand to preserve our food security capacity, in today’s terms that is 15 – 20 billion rand so you can’t talk about 300 million rand to assist us to get through the drought
Script: And if the rains fail again this coming December, the whole of Southern Africa will be in free fall.

metadata.Summary: South Africa is laying the groundwork in case it needs to import as much as 6.2-million tons of maize after successive seasons of drought threaten the crop in Africa's top producer of the grain, which is usually a net exporter. State-run ports and rail company Transet CEO Siyabonga Gama said "the rail side is not the issue. We have the capacity there to absorb that much maize," he said. He said South Africa's ports were designed mostly to export grain rather than import it, but this hurdle could be overcome. The issue is the import silo capacity so there are a few things that we will need to tweak. It could still be done." But he said this when the estimated import was 4000 million tons. There was hope that some planting could be done early in 2016 but 50% of the 2.55 Million hectares wasn't planted and we already had a poor harvest last year so we have very low stocks
metadata.Further information: The outlook is not good as an El Nino weather system is exacerbating a scorching start to the growing season, following drought conditions in the previous one which shrivelled the crop by a third to 9.94-million tons, the lowest since 2007. This is helping to fuel inflation in Africa's most advanced economy as the white variety of maize is a staple that provides much of South Africa's caloric intake. South Africa's central bank has repeatedly voiced its concern this year about the impact of drought and food prices on the inflation outlook. The March maize contract climbed over 2% to an all-time high of R3 662/t on Tuesday after forecast rain over the weekend in the western part of the maize belt failed to meet expectations. The December contract is fetching R3 705/t, up 75% so far in 2015 and in January 2016 it is R5000/t It it is going to be a very big import year. But aside from the main grain facilities at the ports of Durban and East London, South Africa Gama said Port Elizabeth and Cape Town and even Richards Bay, which is mostly used for coal exports could be used. The concern is that the railway lines are not in a good state, and we do not have have insufficient storage capacity. What will these additional import cost do to the already financially over burdened farmers? Zimbabwe has also suffered a massive crop failure and will need to import maize which is likely to have to come through South Africa. There are fears that we could be facing food riots by the end of the year.
